title: Throwing a stoneware baking dish
subtitle: A functional baking dish thrown as a cylinder in grogged stoneware and altered oval at leather-hard, for oven use at cone 6
excerpt: A stoneware baking dish is thrown as a wide, low cylinder in grogged stoneware, then altered at the leather-hard stage by pressing the walls into an oval shape for a classic oven dish format. Grogged stoneware is the right clay for this: the grog (pre-fired clay particles) reduces thermal shock during repeated oven heating and cooling. The finished dish is suitable for oven use at domestic temperatures and moves from fridge to oven without cracking if the transition is gradual.
sourceNotes: Thrown and altered baking dish pattern derived from first principles. Oval alteration technique from studio practice; historical reference in Charles Binns, The Potter's Craft (1922, Van Nostrand). Grogged stoneware thermal shock resistance documented in Ceramic Frequency technical notes.

content.text: A stoneware baking dish is a workhorse piece: it goes from cold storage to a hot oven and sits on the table as a serving dish. It is made from
grogged stoneware
, thrown as a low cylinder roughly 22 cm in diameter and 7 cm tall, then altered at the
leather-hard
stage by pressing the round cylinder wall gently into an oval approximately 28 cm long and 18 cm wide. The low, wide shape is more practical for baking than a deep round bowl.

This is an advanced project for two reasons. First, 1.4 kg of clay needs strong centring and pulling. Second, timing matters for the altering step. The clay must be at the right leather-hard stage. Too wet and the form relaxes back to round as it dries. Too dry and it cracks at the altered points.

attrs.title: Studio safety
attrs.content: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no compressed air, no dry sanding indoors. Ventilation matters: a downdraft vent or open window with an extractor. Wear welder's shade-5 glasses when peephole-watching at high temperatures. Never open a hot kiln below 80 degrees Celsius. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach.

content.text: What you'll need

materials.name: Mid-fire glaze, pre-mixed (food-safe)
materials.quantity: enough to glaze interior and exterior of baking dish

content.text: Preparation

Wedge 1.4 kg of grogged stoneware thoroughly. Grogged clay requires more wedging effort than smooth clay because the grog particles resist the kneading action. Check for any dry patches or uneven texture and continue wedging until the clay is fully homogeneous. Fix a large bat to the wheel head: this size dish cannot be safely removed from the bare wheel head after throwing. Have a long sponge on a stick for removing excess water from the interior during throwing.
Throwing the cylinder

Centre the 1.4 kg lump on the bat. Grogged clay can feel rougher to centre than smooth stoneware: the grog particles create slight resistance under the palm. Use more centring passes and slightly more pressure than you would for smooth clay at the same weight.
Open a wide floor: pull the centre out to 150 mm in diameter, leaving 10 to 12 mm at the base. The baking dish needs a substantial base to distribute heat evenly in the oven.

Pull the walls upward in three passes to a height of 70 mm, keeping wall thickness at 7 to 8 mm. Grogged stoneware is more resistant to pulling thin than smooth stoneware. Do not force the walls thinner than 6 mm: at oven temperatures, a thin-walled baking dish is more vulnerable to thermal shock cracking than a slightly heavier one.

On the final pass, allow the rim to flare very slightly outward, no more than 5 to 10 mm wider than the cylinder body. This slight outward flare will become the rim of the baking dish and gives it a practical lip for gripping with oven gloves.

Smooth the interior and exterior with the wooden rib. Compress the rim with the chamois leather. Check the rim diameter with calipers: target 220 mm. Remove excess water from the interior. Wire off the cylinder on the bat. Mark one point on the rim with the needle tool to track the long axis of the oval you will press.

Cover loosely with plastic and allow to dry to leather-hard. The cylinder should take 12 to 24 hours to reach leather-hard depending on room conditions. Test by pressing a finger gently against the wall: it should feel cool, firm, and slightly damp but should not deform under pressure.
Altering to oval

Place the leather-hard cylinder on the banding wheel. Identify the axis you marked at throwing: this becomes the long axis of the oval. Position the dish so this axis runs front to back on the banding wheel.

Place both palms flat against the wall at the two points that will become the long ends of the oval (90 degrees from the marked long axis). Press gently inward from both sides simultaneously. The cylinder should yield gradually, the long axis stretching outward as the short axis compresses. Work in stages: press 20 mm inward from each side, then rotate the banding wheel 180 degrees and repeat from the other side to keep the pressure even.

Continue in stages until the dish is approximately 280 mm along the long axis and 180 mm along the short axis. Check the oval from above to confirm the shape is symmetrical. Any difference in the two long-axis halves indicates uneven pressure: apply more pressure to the longer half.

Smooth any creases or marks on the outside wall with a damp finger or the metal rib. The inside corners where the oval curves are tightest may show slight wrinkling: smooth these from the inside with a small damp sponge.

Check that the rim is still at an even height all around the oval circumference. Use the needle tool to level any section that has dropped during altering. Allow the altered dish to firm up slightly before trimming.
Trimming

Invert the oval dish onto the wheel head. The oval shape cannot be centred on the spinning wheel in the usual way: instead, place it on a bat and trim by hand using the loop tool on the stationary bat, turning the banding wheel slowly by hand. Trim an oval
foot ring
that follows the oval profile of the dish, approximately 20 mm in from the outer wall all the way around.
Clear clay from inside the foot ring to bring the base interior to an even 8 to 10 mm thickness. Compress the trimmed base surfaces with a damp metal rib.
Smooth the foot ring edges. The foot ring must sit flat on a level surface: test by placing the dish on a flat bat and checking that it does not rock on any of its four quadrants.
Drying

Dry the altered oval dish right-side up on a wire rack. The oval form may attempt to relax back slightly toward round during the final drying stages if any moisture remains in the clay. This movement is minimal on well-grogged stoneware at true leather-hard. Dry evenly and slowly, covered loosely, to
bone-dry
. A large, heavy form like this baking dish benefits from a longer drying period of several days in a studio rather than being accelerated with heat.
Bisque firing
Load the bone-dry baking dish upright on a kiln shelf. It is acceptable to nest smaller bisqueware pieces inside the dish during bisque firing, as long as pieces do not touch the walls.
Bisque
fire to cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius). Use a slow ramp: 40 degrees Celsius per hour to 200 degrees Celsius for the large form, then 100 degrees Celsius per hour to cone 06. Hold 10 minutes at peak.
Glazing and glaze firing

A food-safe, oven-safe mid-fire glaze is required for a functional baking dish. Glaze the interior by pouring and swirling. Dip-glaze or brush the exterior. Leave the foot ring and base unglazed to a 5 mm margin. The interior glaze coat should be even and smooth: an uneven or pitted glaze interior in a baking dish is difficult to clean after use. Glaze-fire to cone 6 (1220 degrees Celsius). Use the same slow initial ramp as the bisque schedule.
Care

Grogged stoneware fired to cone 6 is suitable for oven use at domestic baking temperatures up to 240 degrees Celsius. Do not place the cold dish directly into a very hot oven: allow the dish to reach room temperature before oven entry, or start in a cold oven that heats gradually with the piece inside. Do not place a hot dish on a cold wet surface or in cold water: thermal shock is the risk even with grogged stoneware. The dish is dishwasher-safe. Do not use on an induction hob, gas flame, or direct electric ring.
Variations

A deeper version at 10 cm height from the same 1.4 kg of clay suits gratins and deeper casserole dishes. The altering technique is identical but the oval shape is slightly harder to achieve cleanly on a taller wall: work the altering in more stages.

Individual ramekin-sized baking dishes from 250 g each, altered into small ovals of 12 cm by 8 cm, make a set of crème brûlée or individual gratin dishes. The alteration is the same technique at a smaller scale and the clay requires less pressure to reshape.

rows.problem: Cylinder relaxes back toward round after pressing
rows.cause: Clay still too wet at the altering stage: the wall does not have enough structural strength to hold the oval against the clay's own memory
rows.fix: Wait longer before altering. True leather-hard on a 1.4 kg piece takes 12 to 24 hours. Test by pressing a finger firmly against the wall: it should not deform.

rows.problem: Cracks appear at the corners of the oval during pressing
rows.cause: Clay dried too much at the corners before altering, or pressure applied unevenly with one side pressed significantly further than the other
rows.fix: Work in smaller stages, pressing 10 mm at a time from alternate sides. If the clay is approaching too-dry, mist the exterior lightly and wait 10 minutes before continuing.

rows.problem: Oval foot ring does not sit flat: dish rocks
rows.cause: Foot ring trimmed unevenly around the oval perimeter when trimming on a stationary bat by hand
rows.fix: Use a straight-edge to check the foot ring height at four points around the oval. Where the foot ring is too high, trim it down with the loop tool. Where too low, shim the low corner with a thin coil of soft clay and let it firm before bisque firing.

rows.cause: Grog particles in the clay surface caused small surface voids that were not fully sealed by the glaze coat
rows.fix: Apply a thicker glaze coat to the interior. Grogged stoneware interiors benefit from a slightly heavier glaze application than smooth stoneware. Sieve the glaze and apply at a slightly higher specific gravity.
